svg.title: Elo depends on battle order; Bradley-Terry does not
svg.desc: Four chatbots A, B, C and D fight a round-robin arena, 18 battles total (every pair meets 3 times). The win matrix (row beat column) is A beats B 2, A beats C 3, A beats D 3, B beats A 1, B beats C 2, B beats D 3, C beats A 0, C beats B 1, C beats D 2, D beats A 0, D beats B 0, D beats C 1, giving raw win totals of 8 for A, 6 for B, 3 for C and 1 for D out of 9 games each. Replaying the same 18 battles through Elo (start rating 1000, K factor 32) in the as-listed order gives final ratings A 1083.7, B 1034.8, C 962.2, D 919.2; replaying the identical battles in a shuffled order gives A 1087.2, B 1038.8, C 961.4, D 912.6, a difference of plus 3.5 for A, plus 4.0 for B, minus 0.8 for C and minus 6.6 for D: the same battles produce different numbers depending on order. A single hand-worked Elo update (A beats B, both starting at 1000, K=32) gives expected score E_A = 0.50, so the winner rises to 1016.0 and the loser falls to 984.0. In contrast, fitting a Bradley-Terry model by iterated Zermelo updates on the same aggregate win matrix converges after 20 iterations to strengths A 0.7015, B 0.2314, C 0.0506 and D 0.0164 (from an equal 0.25 start), which implies P(A beats D) = 0.977 and P(B beats C) = 0.821. This ranking, A greater than B greater than C greater than D, is identical for every ordering of the battles, because Bradley-Terry reads only the aggregate totals.
